Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a severe fungal disease that attacks leaves, blossoms, and fruits of apple trees, resulting in characteristic velvety dark olive lesions, defoliation, and cracked or deformed fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety circular spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots may merge, turn olive-black, and cause leaf distortion
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely during midsummer
Dark brown, corky, scabby lesions with defined borders on developing fruit
Severely affected fruits crack open, become stunted, and rot
causes: Fungus Venturia inaequalis overwintering in fallen dead leaves
Release of ascospores during warm, wet spring rains
Prolonged leaf wetness of 6 to 9 hours at moderate temperatures (15-24°C)
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars such as Liberty, Enterprise, or Prima
Prune apple tree canopies annually to improve air circulation and accelerate drying
Rake, chop, or compost fallen autumn leaves to eliminate overwintering spore reservoirs
Apply urea to ground leaves in late autumn to speed decomposition
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (captan, mancozeb) starting at green tip stage
Use post-infection curative systemic fungicides (such as myclobutanil or kresoxim-methyl) when infection conditions are met
Remove severely infected fruitlets during early thinning
Follow regional disease forecast models (Mills table) for spray timing
management: Practice integrated pest management (IPM) with weather monitoring stations
Rotate fungicide chemical classes (FRAC codes) to avoid pathogen resistance
Maintain tree vigor through balanced soil nutrition and water management

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a destructive fungal pathogen that produces frogeye leaf spots, sunken wood cankers, and a firm, concentric black rot on maturing apple fruits.
symptoms: Frogeye leaf spots with purple margins and light brown or tan centers
Circular brown rot expanding rapidly on fruit near the calyx end
Alternating dark and light concentric rings on rotting apples
Infected apples turn completely black, shrivel, and dry into firm mummies
Reddish-brown sunken cankers with peeling bark on limbs and trunks
causes: Fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa surviving in dead twigs, cankers, and mummified fruit
Spores spread by splashing rain, wind, and pruning equipment
Infection facilitated by insect bites, mechanical injury, or sunburn
prevention: Prune out dead, damaged, or cankered branches at least 15 cm below infected tissue
Remove and destroy all mummified apples from trees and orchard floor before spring
Control codling moth and other boring insects that breach fruit cuticles
Prevent winter sunscald and mechanical bark injuries
treatment: Apply protective fungicides such as captan, thiophanate-methyl, or strobilurins from silver tip through harvest
Disinfect pruning tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol between cuts
Prune cankers during dry winter dormancy
management: Eliminate wild alternate hosts like dead oak and wild blackberry nearby
Conduct regular canopy scouting during post-bloom and fruit-fill stages
Maintain adequate irrigation during dry spells to prevent drought stress

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is a heteroecious fungal disease requiring both apple trees and eastern red cedar or juniper trees to complete its complex two-year life cycle.
symptoms: Small, bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface in early spring
Spots enlarge and develop black specks (pycnia) within the orange centers
Tubular, cup-like fungal structures (aecia) protrude from the leaf underside in summer
Yellow or orange blemishes on the calyx end of young apples
Early leaf defoliation and reduced fruit size on susceptible apple cultivars
causes: Fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae
Gelatinous orange horn-like galls on juniper/cedar trees producing teliospores in spring
Windborne spores traveling up to several miles during rainy spring weather
prevention: Plant rust-immune or resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Freedom, Redfree, Enterprise)
Eradicate nearby Juniperus virginiana trees within a 1 to 2 mile perimeter if feasible
Prune and destroy cedar galls on ornamental junipers before orange spore horns emerge in spring
treatment: Apply preventative fungicides containing myclobutanil, mancozeb, or trifloxystrobin from pink bud through petal fall
Treat young expanding apple foliage immediately before predicted spring rain events
management: Monitor local weather conditions and bud development stages
Coordinate landscape management between fruit orchards and surrounding cedar trees
Maintain spray records to alternate fungicide modes of action

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage displays uniform deep green coloration, clear venation, intact leaf margins, and vigorous tissue growth with no signs of fungal, bacterial, or insect damage.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Leaves appear uniform dark green, lustrous, and fully expanded
No spotting, discoloration, curling, or necrosis on leaf blades or petioles
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Continue regular crop monitoring and scouting for early pest or disease symptoms
Maintain good orchard sanitation by removing pruned debris and fallen leaf litter
Ensure balanced soil fertilization based on periodic leaf tissue and soil tests
Provide consistent soil moisture through drip or micro-sprinkler irrigation
treatment: No treatment needed
Continue routine monitoring throughout vegetative and fruiting periods
management: Maintain plant health through balanced annual nitrogen, potassium, and micronutrient applications
Ensure proper canopy open-center or central-leader pruning to maximize sunlight penetration and air movement

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry plant displays healthy, vigorous vegetative growth with characteristic glossy, emerald-green leaves and no evidence of fungal blight, chlorosis, or root rot.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Foliage is evenly green with no interveinal chlorosis or marginal necrosis
Stems are firm, clean, and free of cankers or lesions
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Maintain acidic soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2 using elemental sulfur or acidic fertilizers
Mulch root zones with aged pine bark or sawdust to conserve moisture and suppress weeds
Ensure excellent soil drainage to prevent Phytophthora root rot
Scout regularly for blueberry maggot, mummy berry, and anthracnose
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain regular cultural care and pest surveillance
management: Apply ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizers rather than nitrate forms
Prune older canes annually to stimulate vigorous new basal shoot growth
Ensure consistent drip irrigation, especially during flower bud set and fruit swelling

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of sweet and sour cherry is a pervasive fungal disease characterized by white powdery fungal mycelium on new leaves, shoot tips, and occasionally fruit.
symptoms: Superficial white powdery patches on underside of leaves and young shoot tips
Leaves curl upward, distort, become leathery, and develop chlorotic or necrotic spots
Stunted young terminal shoot growth with shortened internodes
Infected green cherry fruits develop web-like russeting, indentations, or white powdery growth
Tiny dark spherical chasmothecia visible on older infected leaf surfaces in late season
causes: Fungus Podosphaera clandestina overwintering as chasmothecia on leaves, bark, and soil
Spore release stimulated by moderate temperatures (15-25°C) and high relative humidity
Disease thrives in shaded, dense canopies without free surface water
prevention: Prune cherry tree canopies to encourage open air flow and sunlight penetration
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which stimulates excessive tender succulent shoot growth
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that elevates canopy humidity
treatment: Apply sulfur-based or potassium bicarbonate sprays at early sign of infection
Use targeted fungicides such as DMI (triazoles) or QoI (strobilurins) at shuck fall and post-harvest
Apply horticultural mineral oils or neem extract for organic management
management: Rotate fungicide modes of action to prevent fungal resistance
Monitor new sucker and shoot growth weekly throughout the active season
Clean fallen leaves and pruned twigs from beneath cherry trees

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: The cherry foliage exhibits healthy deep green leaves with serrated margins, smooth bark on spurs, and robust shoot elongation free of spots, gummosis, or mildew.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Leaves are robust, lustrous green, and unblemished
Stems, buds, and fruit spurs show no gummosis, cankers, or wilting
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Perform annual dormant pruning to optimize canopy structure and air circulation
Apply copper sprays during dormant season to prevent bacterial canker
Maintain balanced soil fertility and appropriate mulch coverage around the drip line
treatment: No treatment needed
Continue standard preventive orchard maintenance
management: Monitor canopy regularly for insect vectors such as cherry fruit fly and aphids
Practice clean harvesting and avoid bark injuries caused by mechanical harvesters

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is one of the most yield-limiting foliar diseases of maize worldwide, causing distinct rectangular lesions bounded strictly by parallel leaf veins.
symptoms: Small, tan spots with chlorotic halos developing on lower leaves first
Lesions expand into elongated, rectangular grayish-tan spots strictly limited by leaf veins
Mature lesions measure 2 to 7 cm in length and turn gray in humid conditions due to sporulation
Lesions coalesce, blighting entire leaf blades and causing premature senescence
Stalk lodging and reduced grain fill in severe infections
causes: Fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis surviving in corn residue on the soil surface
Warm temperatures (24-32°C) combined with prolonged high relative humidity (>90%)
Continuous no-till or reduced-till corn cropping systems
prevention: Select high-yielding corn hybrids with high genetic tolerance or resistance to gray leaf spot
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like soybean, alfalfa, or small grains
Tillage management to bury or accelerate the decomposition of infected corn residue
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins, or SDHI premixes) between VT (tasseling) and R2 (blister) stages
Prioritize fungicide application when disease is observed on the third leaf below the ear prior to tasseling
management: Scout fields weekly starting two weeks before tasseling
Evaluate local disease pressure, hybrid susceptibility, and commodity prices before spraying
Implement balanced nitrogen and potassium fertilization to support stalk integrity

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is a fungal disease of maize producing cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces, causing leaf tissue death and reduced photosynthesis.
symptoms: Small, powdery cinnamon-brown pustules (uredinia) scattered across upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, revealing reddish-brown fungal spores
Lesions turn brownish-black late in the season as teliospores form
Chlorosis and necrosis surrounding heavy clusters of pustules
Severe infections lead to leaf death, stunted plant growth, and diminished kernel fill
causes: Fungus Puccinia sorghi
Wind-transported urediniospores carried northward on southerly storm systems
Cool to moderate temperatures (16-25°C) and high relative humidity (near 100%)
prevention: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids with specific Rp resistance genes
Plant early in the season to enable grain maturity before heavy spore loads arrive
Avoid excessive planting densities that prolong leaf wetness
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides (such as azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, or propiconazole) if rust appears before tasseling on susceptible hybrids
Spray when pustules cover 5% or more of the upper canopy leaf area
management: Regularly scout field borders and lower canopies during cool, dewy weather
Maintain diverse genetics in cropping operations to prevent single-gene resistance breakdown

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern corn leaf blight is a devastating foliar disease recognized by large, cigar-shaped, grayish-green to tan lesions that can cause rapid blighting of corn canopies.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped lesions (2 to 15 cm long and 1 to 2 cm wide)
Lesions start as grayish-green, water-soaked streaks that turn tan or buff with age
Dark olive or black velvety fungal sporulation on lesion surfaces under humid conditions
Lesions merge, destroying vast areas of green leaf tissue
Severe premature plant senescence and significant grain weight reduction
causes: Fungus Exserohilum turcicum (syn. Setosphaeria turcica)
Overwinters as mycelia and chlamydospores in infected corn crop debris
Moderate temperatures (18-27°C) accompanied by extended periods of heavy dew and rain
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids containing Ht resistance genes (Ht1, Ht2, Ht3, or HtN)
Practice 1- to 2-year crop rotation out of corn into soybeans or legumes
Incorporate infected corn stover into the soil after harvest to promote decay
treatment: Apply systemic foliar fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins) at tasseling or early silking
Treat when lesions are present on or near the ear leaf around silking time
management: Conduct regular field scouting from V8 stage through milk stage (R3)
Track regional disease occurrences and forecast risk factors
Maintain adequate soil potassium levels to improve natural crop defense

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The maize plant exhibits dark green, robust leaf blades with clean parallel venation, sturdy stalks, and normal vegetative or reproductive development.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Leaves are deep green, upright, and free of lesions or rust pustules
Stalks are sturdy with clean nodes and strong root bracing
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Implement balanced nutrient programs matching target yield goals
Practice routine crop scouting throughout early vegetative and reproductive stages
Ensure proper planting depth and uniform plant spacing to minimize competition
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain standard agronomic surveillance
management: Maintain soil organic matter and optimize irrigation scheduling
Keep records of field history and hybrid performance

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is an extremely destructive fungal disease of grapes in warm, humid climates, capable of causing complete crop loss by rotting grape clusters into shriveled black mummies.
symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with dark margins and tiny black dots (pycnidia) in a ring
Elongated, sunken black lesions on shoots, petioles, and tendrils
Soft, light-brown spots appearing on infected berries, rapidly expanding to engulf the entire berry
Infected berries shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies within a few days
Mummified berries remain tightly attached to the fruit cluster
causes: Fungus Guignardia bidwellii overwintering in mummified berries and cane cankers
Ascospores and conidia discharged during rainy spring periods
Optimum infection occurs between 21°C and 27°C with continuous moisture
prevention: Prune and destroy all mummified berries hanging on vines and on the ground during winter
Maintain canopy training systems that provide maximum ventilation and sunlight exposure
Remove suckers and weed growth beneath the trellis to improve airflow
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (mancozeb, captan, or ziram) from early shoot development (1-3 inches) through bloom
Apply systemic fungicides (myclobutanil, tebuconazole, or kresoxim-methyl) from pre-bloom to 4 weeks post-bloom
Ensure continuous chemical protection during warm rainfall events
management: Scout vineyards closely starting at bud break through veraison
Alternate fungicide chemistries to prevent pathogen tolerance
Maintain good vineyard weed control to lower ground humidity

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).scientific_name: Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, Fomitiporia mediterranea
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca, also known as black measles, is a complex fungal grapevine trunk disease that causes characteristic tiger-stripe interveinal leaf patterns, berry spotting, and wood vascular dieback.
symptoms: Distinct 'tiger-stripe' pattern on leaves: interveinal yellowing and necrosis with green veins
Small, dark purplish or brown spots ('measles') sprinkled over berry skins
Severe cases cause sudden vine collapse and wilting during hot summer days (apoplexy)
Dark brown or black vascular streaking inside infected woody trunks
Spongy white heart rot in the center of mature vine trunks
causes: Fungal complex including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, and wood-decay basidiomycetes
Spores infect vines through open pruning wounds made during wet winter months
Toxins produced by the fungi translocate to foliage and fruit
prevention: Delay pruning until late winter when wound healing is rapid and spore dispersal is lower
Apply pruning wound sealants or biological protectants (Trichoderma spp.) immediately after cutting
Avoid large pruning cuts that expose extensive cross-sections of woody tissue
Purchase certified disease-free nursery stock
treatment: Prune affected arms or cordons well below diseased wood (re-training trunk renewal)
There are no effective chemical curative sprays for systemic trunk vascular infections
Perform remedial vine surgery or trunk renewal for salvageable vines
management: Mark and map symptomatic vines in mid-to-late summer for targeted winter remedial pruning
Sterilize shears between cuts when removing infected vines
Remove and incinerate dead vines and old cordons from the vineyard

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Grape leaf blight, caused by Pseudocercospora vitis, produces irregular brown angular lesions on foliage, causing early defoliation, weakened vines, and delayed berry ripening.
symptoms: Irregular, angular, reddish-brown to dark brown leaf spots delimited by smaller veins
Faint olivaceous or grayish moldy growth on the underside of spots in humid weather
Lesions coalesce into large necrotic blights across leaf lobes
Infected leaves curl, dry out, and drop prematurely in late summer
Reduced grape cluster sweetness and diminished vine carbohydrate reserves
causes: Fungus Pseudocercospora vitis (syn. Phaeoisariopsis vitis / Isariopsis clavispora)
Overwinters on infected fallen leaves and dormant vine canes
Favored by warm temperatures, high humidity, and dense shaded canopies
prevention: Canopy management including shoot thinning, leaf pulling, and shoot positioning
Prompt removal and incorporation or burning of post-harvest leaf litter
Maintain adequate spacing between rows to facilitate wind penetration
treatment: Apply protective broad-spectrum fungicides (such as copper hydroxide or mancozeb)
Include strobilurin or DMI fungicides in standard seasonal spray programs
Spray during late summer when leaf blight pressure typically escalates
management: Coordinate leaf blight control with downy mildew and powdery mildew spray schedules
Scout mid-canopy leaves during midsummer and after harvest
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation

Grape___healthy.description: The grapevine exhibits pristine, vibrant green palmate foliage with well-formed tendrils, smooth canes, and healthy expanding grape clusters free of spotting or decay.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Leaves are uniform green, crisp, and actively photosynthesizing
Canes, cordons, and fruit clusters are clean and vigorous
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Continue regular canopy management including shoot positioning and sucker removal
Implement proactive powdery mildew and downy mildew monitoring programs
Maintain balanced vine nutrition and petiole nutrient analysis
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain routine viticultural scouting
management: Use deficit irrigation strategies to balance vegetative growth and fruit quality
Prune systematically during dormancy to maintain vine balance

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB) or Citrus Greening is one of the most destructive citrus diseases in the world, vectored by the Asian citrus psyllid, leading to tree decline, bitter misshapen fruit, and tree death.
symptoms: Asymmetric, blotchy mottle chlorosis across leaf blades (not matching vein patterns)
Yellowing of individual shoots or branches ('yellow shoots') against green canopy
Leaves become small, upright, leathery, and develop thickened, corky veins
Fruit remains small, lopsided, poorly colored (green at bottom), and bitter or sour
Fruit contains aborted dark seeds and drops prematurely from the tree
Progressive canopy dieback, root starvation, and tree mortality within 3 to 5 years
causes: Phloem-limited unculturable bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus
Transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) during feeding
Spread through grafting with infected propagation budwood
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free citrus trees from screened indoor nurseries
Control Asian citrus psyllid populations using systemic and foliar insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid)
Install physical insect exclusion screens in high-value or commercial nursery production
Enforce quarantine restrictions preventing movement of citrus plant material
treatment: There is currently no cure for infected trees; prompt removal and destruction of infected trees is recommended to protect neighbors
Apply intensive foliar nutritional sprays (zinc, manganese, iron, potassium) to prolong productive life
Oxytetracycline trunk injection where legally registered and approved
management: Implement regional psyllid control coordination across citrus groves
Scout monthly using tap sampling to detect psyllids and visual surveys for blotchy mottle
Promote biological control using parasitoid wasps (Tamarixia radiata)

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot affects peach foliage, twigs, and fruit, producing a characteristic 'shot-hole' appearance on leaves, deep fruit pitting, and twig dieback.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown or black
Centers of leaf spots drop out, leaving a ragged 'shot-hole' appearance
Leaf yellowing and extensive early summer defoliation
Dark brown, sunken, cracked, and gum-exuding pits on developing peaches
Spring and summer cankers on succulent twigs leading to tip dieback
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni
Overwinters in twig cankers and terminal bud scales
Spread by wind-driven rain, dew, and sandy soils blowing against plant tissue
prevention: Plant bacterial spot-resistant peach cultivars (e.g., Candor, Dixired, Clayton)
Establish windbreaks in sandy soils to minimize abrasive windblown sand damage
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that promotes late succulent growth
treatment: Apply dormant and delayed-dormant copper sprays to reduce bacterial overwintering inoculum
Use low-rate fixed copper or oxytetracycline sprays from shuck split through cover sprays
Prune out infected twigs during dry winter weather
management: Monitor weather forecasts for wind and rainstorms
Exercise caution with copper rates during warm spring to prevent copper phytotoxicity on foliage
Maintain overall orchard health and uniform soil moisture

Peach___healthy.description: The peach tree displays healthy lanceolate leaves with deep green color, intact leaf blades without shot-holes, sturdy new wood growth, and clean developing fruit.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Leaves are lanceolate, vibrant green, and unblemished
Bark is clean with no cankers, gummosis, or twig dieback
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Maintain open-center vase pruning to enhance air movement and light
Perform preventative dormant sprays for peach leaf curl and bacterial canker
Scout systematically for oriental fruit moth, peach tree borer, and brown rot
treatment: No treatment needed
Continue standard seasonal orchard management
management: Thin young peach fruitlets early to ensure superior fruit size and prevent limb breakage
Maintain balanced irrigation through drip lines during the final fruit swell

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of bell pepper is a major destructive disease causing necrotic foliar lesions, leaf drop, sunscald susceptibility, and unmarketable blistered fruit.
symptoms: Small, circular or irregular, water-soaked spots on leaves turning dark brown or black
Lesions on lower leaf surface often have a pale or glistening center with a greasy look
Widespread leaf yellowing and rapid severe defoliation, exposing fruit to sunscald
Small, raised, blister-like or wart-like rough spots on green fruit
Fruit spots turn brown, enlarge, and become cracked or scabby
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas euvesicatoria (and related Xanthomonas species)
Transmitted through contaminated seed, transplants, and crop residue
Favored by warm temperatures (24-30°C) and heavy rainfall or overhead irrigation
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water-treated seed and certified transplants
Select bell pepper varieties with genetic resistance to bacterial spot races (1-10)
Rotate crops out of solanaceous plants (tomatoes, eggplants, peppers) for at least 2 to 3 years
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers
treatment: Apply copper bactericides combined with mancozeb for improved bacterial control
Apply systemic acquired resistance (SAR) inducers such as acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard)
Use bacteriophage treatments or biofungicides (Bacillus subtilis) in integrated programs
management: Sanitize field equipment, stakes, and greenhouse trays with chlorine or quaternary ammonia
Avoid handling or cultivating pepper plants when leaves are wet
Plow under or destroy crop residues immediately following the final harvest

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: The bell pepper plant exhibits lush, rich green foliage, robust branching stems, strong flower set, and clean, glossy fruit free of blemishes or bacterial lesions.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Foliage is broad, vibrant green, and free of chlorotic spots or necrotic margins
Fruits are firm, glossy, well-shaped, and unblemished
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture to prevent blossom end rot and stress
Use plastic or organic mulches to stabilize soil temperatures and reduce weed pressure
Scout regularly for aphids, thrips, and pepper weevils
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain standard agronomic care
management: Provide balanced calcium and potassium fertilization
Maintain proper row spacing to optimize ventilation between pepper rows

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease of potatoes that attacks mature foliage, characterized by distinct concentric 'target-board' lesions that cause leaf necrosis and reduced tuber yields.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black spots appearing first on older lower leaves
Lesions enlarge to produce distinct concentric ridges resembling a target board
Narrow yellow chlorotic halo surrounding individual necrotic lesions
Severe infections cause leaves to yellow, wither, and die while hanging on the stem
Tubers develop brown, sunken, dry, leathery lesions with raised purple margins
causes: Fungus Alternaria solani surviving in solanaceous plant residue and volunteer potatoes
Spores spread by wind, splashing rain, and mechanical cultivation
Favored by alternating wet and dry conditions and stressed, aging potato vines
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (cereals, legumes, corn) for 2 to 3 years
Select moderately resistant potato varieties (e.g., Ranger Russet, Dakota Rose)
Maintain plant vigor through adequate nitrogen and potassium fertilization
Avoid overhead irrigation during late afternoon or evening
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) starting before vine canopy closure
Apply translaminar or systemic fungicides (azoxystrobin, boscalid, difenoconazole) when disease appears
Kill potato vines completely before harvesting to reduce tuber skinning and spore transmission
management: Monitor lower leaves weekly starting at tuber initiation
Handle harvested tubers carefully to prevent bruises and cure at 10-13°C and high humidity
Destroy potato cull piles before spring planting

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a catastrophic oomycete disease responsible for the Irish Potato Famine, capable of rapidly destroying entire fields of potato foliage and decaying tubers into foul, rotting masses.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale-to-dark green irregular lesions rapidly expanding into large brown-black blights
Delicate white cottony mildew growth visible on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Dark brown to black lesions on petioles and stems causing plant collapse
Tubers show shallow copper-brown or purplish sunken skin discoloration
Granular reddish-brown dry rot extending into tuber flesh, often followed by foul soft rot
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans surviving in infected seed tubers or cull piles
Wind-dispersed sporangia traveling several miles in overcast, humid weather
Favored by cool, wet conditions: temperatures of 12-21°C and relative humidity >90%
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers
Destroy all cull potato piles, volunteer potato plants, and solanaceous weeds (nightshade)
Select late blight-resistant potato cultivars (e.g., Defender, Sarpo Mira)
Hill soil deeply over potato rows to create a barrier preventing sporangia from washing onto tubers
treatment: Apply preventative fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, fluazinam) on a strict 5-7 day schedule during high risk periods
Apply targeted oomycete fungicides (mandipropamid, cyazofamid, metalaxyl/mefenoxam) upon disease confirmation
Kill vines chemically or mechanically at least 2 to 3 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber contamination
management: Utilize computer-based late blight forecast systems (e.g., Blitecast) to time treatments
Immediately rogue out and bag/destroy hot spots of infection within the field
Store harvested potatoes under cool, dry, well-ventilated conditions

Potato___healthy.description: The potato plant displays lush, emerald foliage, sturdy upright stems, full compound leaves with crisp margins, and healthy root and tuber development.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Compound leaves are fully formed, dark green, and free of blemishes or halos
Stems are firm and vigorous with no darkening or water-soaked lesions
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture during tuber bulking to avoid cracking and scab
Keep rows hilled adequately to prevent tuber greening from sun exposure
Scout fields continuously for Colorado potato beetle, aphids, and foliar blights
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain standard agronomic care
management: Follow nutrient testing recommendations for nitrogen and phosphorus balance
Plan harvest timing according to skin set maturity

Raspberry___healthy.description: The raspberry plant shows vigorous primocanes and floricanes, vibrant green compound leaves with serrate edges, clean canes free of spur blight or anthracnose, and robust berry formation.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Compound leaves are vibrant green and completely unblemished
Canes are clean, firm, and free of sunken lesions, cracks, or wilting
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Trellis canes to keep foliage off the ground and maximize sun penetration
Prune out spent floricanes immediately after summer harvest
Maintain adequate plant spacing to allow rapid drying of leaves after rain or dew
treatment: No treatment needed
Continue routine cane fruit maintenance
management: Apply organic mulch around cane bases to moderate soil moisture and root temperatures
Ensure well-drained soil to protect vulnerable root crowns against Phytophthora rot

Soybean___healthy.description: The soybean crop demonstrates dark green, healthy trifoliate leaves, strong nodulation on roots, vigorous branching, and clean pods free of fungal or bacterial lesions.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Trifoliate leaves are uniform rich green without chlorosis, spots, or mottling
Stems and leaf petioles are clean and erect
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum before planting for optimal biological nitrogen fixation
Rotate with non-host crops like corn or sorghum
Monitor fields regularly for soybean aphid, sudden death syndrome, and frogeye leaf spot
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain standard agronomic care
management: Maintain weed-free conditions during critical early canopy establishment
Ensure proper row spacing to balance early ground cover with canopy ventilation

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew is a ubiquitous fungal disease of squash and other cucurbits, spreading as talcum powder-like white spots over leaves and stems, resulting in premature defoliation and poor fruit quality.
symptoms: White, talcum-powder-like circular fungal spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Spots expand rapidly to coalesce and blanket entire leaves, petioles, and young stems
Infected leaves turn yellow, then brown, become dry and brittle, and die prematurely
Loss of foliage exposes squash fruit to sunscald and causes premature ripening
Fruit from heavily infected vines lacks flavor, sweetness, and storability
causes: Fungi Podosphaera xanthii (syn. Sphaerotheca fuliginea) and Erysiphe cichoracearum
Airborne conidia carried over large distances by wind currents
Favored by dense canopies, shade, moderate temperatures (20-27°C), and high humidity without free water
prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant squash cultivars (look for PMR labeling)
Plant in full sun with adequate plant spacing to encourage air movement
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which causes dense, succulent canopy growth
treatment: Apply preventative fungicides at the very first sign of small white spots on lower leaves
Use potassium bicarbonate, sulfur, or horticultural neem oil sprays for organic production
Apply targeted systemic fungicides (such as quinoxyfen, triflumizole, or boscalid) in conventional rotations
management: Rotate chemical classes (FRAC groups) at every application to prevent rapid fungal resistance
Scout undersides of older crown leaves twice weekly
Plow under or remove cucurbit crop debris immediately after harvest

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch is a common fungal disease of strawberries producing numerous small purplish spots that coalesce, causing the leaf tissue to brown, curl upwards, and appear scorched by heat or drought.
symptoms: Small, dark purple, irregular or angular spots developing on upper leaf surfaces
Spots do not develop white or gray centers, distinguishing them from common leaf spot
Spots multiply and coalesce, causing entire leaves to turn dark purple, brown, and dry
Leaves curl upward at the margins, exhibiting a burnt or 'scorched' appearance
Lesions can also infect petioles, runners, fruit sepals (calyx), and fruit stems
Severe infections lead to unmarketable 'dead cap' fruit and reduced runner production
causes: Fungus Diplocarpon earlianum overwintering on infected living leaves and plant debris
Conidia released and splashed by water droplets during warm spring rains
Extended periods of leaf wetness at temperatures between 20°C and 25°C
prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry crowns
Select resistant or tolerant strawberry cultivars (e.g., Honeoye, Allstar)
Renovate matted strawberry beds annually by mowing, narrowing rows, and removing old leaf debris
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers to keep foliage dry
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (captan, thiram) in early spring as new foliage emerges
Apply systemic fungicides (pyraclostrobin, thiophanate-methyl) before bloom if disease history is severe
Rogue out and destroy heavily infected older plants during post-harvest renovation
management: Maintain weed-free beds to maximize air circulation and sunlight exposure
Avoid planting strawberries in poorly drained, low-lying, or foggy field locations
Rotate strawberry plantings to new soil beds every 3 to 4 years

Strawberry___healthy.description: The strawberry plant shows healthy trifoliate leaves with vibrant green luster, clean petioles, strong crown development, active runnering, and firm unblemished berries.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Leaves are robust, lustrous green, and free of purple spots, scorch, or powdery mold
Crowns, runners, and flowers are clean and vigorous
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Mulch strawberry beds with clean straw to elevate fruit and leaves above bare soil
Maintain appropriate spacing between mother and daughter plants to prevent overcrowding
Regularly scout for spider mites, slugs, botrytis gray mold, and leaf scorch
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain standard horticultural care
management: Provide uniform drip irrigation during flowering and fruit ripening
Renovate June-bearing beds promptly after the final harvest

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is a widespread bacterial disease affecting all aboveground tomato parts, producing small water-soaked dark spots on leaves, extensive defoliation, and scabbed, blistered fruit lesions.
symptoms: Small (less than 3 mm), dark, water-soaked, circular or angular spots on foliage
Lesions on leaves turn black, become greasy, and develop a narrow yellow halo
Severely spotted leaves turn yellow, wither, and drop, exposing developing tomatoes to sunscald
Small, raised, black blisters on green fruit that enlarge, become brown, sunken, and scab-like
Elongated dark streaks on stems and petioles
causes: Bacteria Xanthomonas vesicatoria, X. euvesicatoria, X. gardneri, and X. perforans
Survives on infected seed, volunteer tomato plants, and crop residue
Spread by wind-blown rain, overhead irrigation, and handling wet plants
Favored by warm temperatures (24-30°C) and high humidity
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water-treated seed and healthy transplants
Rotate out of solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, eggplants) for at least 2 to 3 years
Implement drip irrigation and avoid overhead sprinkling
Disinfect greenhouse benches, trays, and stakes with 10% bleach solution
treatment: Apply preventative copper sprays mixed with mancozeb for improved bacterial suppression
Apply plant defense activators like acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard)
Utilize registered bacteriophage products (OmniLytics AgriPhage) during active growth
management: Do not cultivate, prune, or harvest tomato plants when leaves are wet with rain or dew
Plow under or destroy crop debris immediately following the harvest season
Scout nursery transplants meticulously before setting into field rows

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is one of the most common fungal diseases of tomato, producing characteristic dark brown concentric 'target-board' lesions on leaves, collar rot on stems, and leathery sunken fruit rot.
symptoms: Circular brown-black spots with concentric rings ('target-board' pattern) on older lower leaves
Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding lesions
Leaves turn yellow, dry out, and drop prematurely, progressing upwards from the base
Dark brown, sunken, concentric lesions at the stem end of green or ripe fruit
Dark, sunken, elongated collar rot cankers on stems of young plants
causes: Fungus Alternaria solani surviving in solanaceous plant debris and volunteer tomatoes
Spreads by windborne spores, splashing rain, and mechanical contact
Favored by warm temperatures (24-29°C) and alternating periods of rain and dry weather
prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (beans, corn, brassicas)
Prune lower leaves (bottom 30 cm) after first fruit cluster forms to prevent soil splash
Mulch soil beneath plants with black plastic or clean straw
Provide wide row spacing and stake or cage plants to promote rapid drying
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper) before symptoms appear or at first spot
Apply systemic fungicides (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, or difenoconazole) if disease spreads
Remove and bag infected lower leaves as soon as first spots appear
management: Water at the base of the plant using drip irrigation or soaker hoses
Clean up and compost or burn all tomato vines at season end
Maintain plant vigor through steady soil moisture and balanced nutrition

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a fast-moving, devastating oomycete pathogen capable of killing tomato plants within days and turning entire fruit crops into foul, rotting mush under cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked grayish-green spots rapidly turning dark brown or black
White fungal-like downy sporulation visible on the underside of infected leaves in humid weather
Brown to black greasy-looking lesions on petioles and main stems, leading to branch collapse
Firm, large, greasy, golden-brown to dark brown rough lesions on green and ripening fruit
Whole plant exhibits sudden wilt, blighting, and foul odor as secondary rots invade
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans surviving in live infected tissue and volunteer potatoes
Microscopic sporangia and zoospores carried by wind and storm fronts over tens of miles
Thrives in cool, wet weather: temperatures of 15-22°C and high humidity (>90%)
prevention: Plant late blight-resistant tomato cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant, Plum Regal)
Do not plant tomatoes in close proximity to potato crops or cull piles
Ensure maximum air circulation with proper staking, caging, and generous plant spacing
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; always use drip irrigation
treatment: Apply preventative fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) on a proactive weekly schedule in high-risk weather
Apply specialized translaminar/systemic oomycete fungicides (mandipropamid, cyazofamid, dimethomorph) immediately upon confirmed regional outbreak
Pull and completely bag infected plants to prevent airborne spore dissemination to neighboring gardens
management: Subscribe to regional late blight alert systems (e.g., USAblight) for local outbreaks
Destroy and do not compost severely infected plant material
Inspect plants twice weekly during periods of persistent overcast, foggy, or rainy weather

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is a prominent fungal disease predominantly affecting greenhouse and high-tunnel tomatoes, causing pale yellow spots on upper leaves and velvety olive-brown mold on the undersides.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish indistinct spots on upper surface of older leaves
Plush, velvety olive-green to grayish-brown fungal growth directly beneath spots on leaf undersides
Infected leaves turn entirely yellow, curl, wither, and drop prematurely
Disease progresses from oldest lower leaves up into the canopy
Blossoms may be blighted and drop; fruit rarely shows dark leathery rot at the stem end
causes: Fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum)
Survives as conidia or sclerotia on crop residue, greenhouse framework, and seed
Thrives in high relative humidity (>85%) and moderate temperatures (21-24°C); common in tunnels
prevention: Maximize ventilation and airflow in high tunnels and greenhouses with exhaust fans and horizontal airflow fans
Keep relative humidity below 85% by heating and venting greenhouse air during evening hours
Plant tomato varieties with genetic resistance (Cf resistance genes)
Water exclusively at soil level with drip irrigation to keep foliage bone dry
treatment: Apply fungicides such as chlorothalonil, copper compounds, or cyazofamid at first symptom onset
Apply biofungicides containing Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Trichoderma species
Prune out infected lower leaves to improve air circulation
management: Thoroughly clean and disinfect greenhouse structures, trellising strings, and tools between crops
Space plants generously to avoid dense tangled canopies
Remove all crop debris promptly at the end of the production cycle

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is one of the most destructive foliar diseases of field tomatoes, causing myriad small circular spots with dark margins and ash-gray centers, resulting in progressive bottom-up defoliation.
symptoms: Numerous small (1.5 to 3 mm), circular spots appearing first on lower, older leaves
Spots have dark brown borders and ash-gray or tan centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) clearly visible in the gray centers of mature spots
Leaves turn yellow, wither, become brown, and drop off
Severe bottom-up defoliation leaves tomatoes exposed to sunscald; fruit itself is rarely infected directly
causes: Fungus Septoria lycopersici surviving in overwintered solanaceous crop debris and nightshade weeds
Pycnidiospores spread primarily by splashing rain, overhead irrigation, and field workers
Favored by warm temperatures (20-25°C) and prolonged leaf wetness
prevention: Practice 2- to 3-year crop rotation out of solanaceous crops
Mulch soil around plants with straw or plastic to prevent spore splash from soil onto lower foliage
Prune the lower 25-30 cm of foliage to eliminate ground contact
Eradicate horsenettle and wild nightshade weeds around the field border
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper octanoate) on a 7- to 10-day schedule
Apply strobilurins (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin) or SDHI fungicides if infection intensifies
Remove and discard heavily infected lower leaves early in the season
management: Use drip irrigation exclusively and never work in tomato fields when leaves are wet
Stake and prune plants to maximize air circulation and sun exposure
Till under or deeply bury crop residue immediately after the final harvest

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny arachnid pests that pierce plant cell walls to suck out chlorophyll, causing fine stippling, bronzing, extensive fine webbing, and severe canopy decline in hot, dry conditions.
symptoms: Fine, pale yellow or white speckling (stippling) on the upper surface of leaves
Leaves become bronzed, bleached, or chlorotic and dry out prematurely
Delicate, silky webbing on the undersides of leaves and spanning across stem nodes and growing tips
Tiny, moving yellow, green, or red mites with two dark lateral spots visible with a hand lens
Stunted vine growth, premature leaf drop, and sunburned or distorted fruit
causes: Arachnid pest Tetranychus urticae
Favored by hot, dry, dusty environmental conditions (temperatures >30°C)
Broad-spectrum insecticide use that destroys natural beneficial predatory mites
prevention: Keep roadways and field paths watered or mulched to reduce airborne dust
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids and organophosphates that decimate natural predators
Maintain adequate irrigation to prevent water-stressed, drought-stressed host plants
treatment: Release predatory mites such as Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus in greenhouse or tunnel settings
Apply insecticidal soaps or horticultural oils, ensuring thorough coverage of leaf undersides
Apply selective miticides (bifenazate, abamectin, or spiromesifen) when economic thresholds are breached
management: Scout leaf undersides weekly with a 10x hand lens, especially along dusty field edges
Overhead misting can temporarily discourage mite population explosions in protected culture
Remove heavily infested individual plants to prevent rapid migration

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is a fungal disease affecting leaves, stems, and fruit of tomato plants, forming pinpoint lesions that expand into dark brown zonate circular spots with prominent concentric rings.
symptoms: Small, brown, pinpoint spots on upper leaf surfaces expanding to circular lesions (5 to 10 mm)
Lesions develop dark brown concentric rings with pale brown or tan centers
Yellow chlorotic halos frequently surround mature leaf lesions
Lesions coalesce, causing large necrotic blights, leaf curling, and premature defoliation
Fruit develops small, circular, sunken brown lesions that crack and form dark fungal crusts
causes: Fungus Corynespora cassiicola surviving on crop debris, weeds, and alternate crop hosts (papaya, soybean)
Conidia dispersed by wind and rain splashes
Favored by warm temperatures (20-30°C) accompanied by extended periods of high relative humidity
prevention: Ensure wide plant spacing and rigorous staking to optimize air circulation and sunlight
Avoid overhead irrigation and keep leaf wetness duration to an absolute minimum
Rotate fields with non-host crops like corn or small grains
Eliminate weed hosts around tomato field perimeters
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) starting before canopy closure
Apply systemic fungicides (fluopyram, boscalid, or azoxystrobin) under active disease pressure
Prune out symptomatic lower foliage early in the infection cycle
management: Scout field interiors and lower canopy leaves regularly
Alternate fungicide FRAC codes to prevent the development of resistant fungal strains
Plow under plant debris deeply after harvest to accelerate decomposition

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is an economically devastating begomovirus transmitted exclusively by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), causing extreme stunting, leaf curling, and near-total crop loss.
symptoms: Severe upward cupping and curling of leaf margins ('spooning')
Marked interveinal and marginal chlorosis (yellowing) of young terminal leaves
Significant reduction in leaf size, giving leaves a crumpled, distorted appearance
Extreme plant stunting with shortened internodes producing a bushy, erect canopy
Heavy flower abscission (drop) and virtually no fruit set if infected prior to flowering
Existing fruit remains small, hard, and unmarketable
causes: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (family Geminiviridae, genus Begomovirus)
Transmitted persistently by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Not mechanically transmitted through seed or pruning tools
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato hybrids (e.g., Tygress, Charger, Invictus)
Install fine insect-proof exclusion netting (50-mesh) on greenhouse and nursery sidewalls
Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulches to disorient and repel flying whiteflies
Establish a mandatory 2- to 3-month host-free crop break between tomato growing seasons
treatment: There is no chemical cure for virus-infected plants; immediately rogue and destroy infected plants
Control whitefly vectors using systemic insecticides (e.g., dinotefuran, imidacloprid) at transplanting
Rotate foliar insecticides (spiromesifen, cyantraniliprole, pyriproxyfen) to suppress whitefly nymphs and adults
management: Monitor whitefly populations with yellow sticky cards placed throughout the field
Control broadleaf weed hosts (e.g., Datura, Solanum nigrum) that serve as virus reservoirs
Bag and remove symptomatic plants in airtight bags before discarding to contain whiteflies

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus is an exceptionally stable and contagious tobamovirus that causes light and dark green mottled foliage, distorted 'shoestring' leaves, internal browning of fruit, and stunted plant growth.
symptoms: Mottling of leaves with alternating light and dark green mosaic patches
Leaf distortion, blistering, twisting, and fern-like or 'shoestring' malformation
Stunted plant growth and reduced canopy size
Uneven ripening of fruit with internal brown necrotic vascular rings (internal browning)
Yellow blotches and brown sunken rings on the skin of ripe tomatoes
causes: Tomato mosaic virus (genus Tobamovirus)
Extremely stable virus that easily spreads mechanically via hands, pruning shears, stakes, and clothing
Can persist in dry crop debris, contaminated seed coats, and root residues in soil for years
Can be introduced through contaminated tobacco products handled by field workers
prevention: Plant certified disease-free, heat-treated or trisodium phosphate-treated seed
Select tomato cultivars with genetic resistance to ToMV (designated with 'T' or 'ToMV')
Enforce strict hand hygiene: wash hands with 20% nonfat dry milk or soapy water before touching plants
Prohibit the use of tobacco products in and around tomato fields or greenhouses
treatment: There are no antiviral chemical sprays; infected plants must be carefully removed and incinerated
Do not touch adjacent healthy plants when roguing out infected specimens
Soak pruning tools in a 20% nonfat dry milk solution or 10% household bleach between plants
management: Steam or solarize soil in contaminated greenhouse beds between seasons
Disinfect all stakes, cages, and trellising wires with virucidal solutions before reuse
Remove solanaceous weeds (nightshade, groundcherry) from field borders

Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato plant exhibits dark green, robust compound foliage, strong thick main stems, vibrant yellow blossoms, and clean, glossy green and ripening fruit free of spots, blemishes, or wilt.
symptoms: No disease symptoms observed
Compound foliage is lush, dark green, and free of chlorotic halos or necrotic lesions
Stems are firm, hirsute, and strong with no cankers or bacterial streaking
Flowers and fruit are abundant, uniform, and unblemished
causes: N/A - Plant appears healthy
prevention: Maintain consistent drip irrigation to avoid blossom-end rot and fruit cracking
Stake, cage, or trellis plants to keep all foliage and fruit elevated above the soil
Prune suckers and lower leaf branches to promote optimal canopy air movement
Scout foliage twice weekly for early signs of hornworms, aphids, blights, or viruses
treatment: No treatment needed
Maintain standard horticultural care and monitoring
management: Apply balanced tomato fertilizers with adequate calcium, magnesium, and potassium
Rotate planting beds each season to maintain long-term soil health
